rashi:a1.1: Libations that are brought by themselves: for example, they brought a communal offering today and did not bring the libations with it, and they brought them the next day. As the Master said (Menaḥot 44b): “Their meal offering and their libations,” even at night; “their meal offering and their libations,” even the next day.
rashi:a1.2: Eating and drinking: the offering and the libations.
tosafot:a1.1: Libations that are brought by themselves, do they require song or not: meaning, the libations of a communal offering that were not offered on its day, and are offered the next day, as we expound (Menaḥot 44b): “And their meal offering,” even up to ten days. One cannot explain it as a case where a person donated a meal offering of libations, for even when they bring an obligatory offering, his [an individual’s] offering does not require libations [the sense appears to be: song]. And it certainly speaks of offering them by day; but offering them at night, Rabbi Elazar has already said: Just as atonement is by day, so song is by day.
gershom:a1.1: Libations that come by themselves: as we say in tractate Menaḥot (44): One who says, “I take upon myself [to bring] wine,” may not bring less than three log.
gershom:a2.1: [Or perhaps] over the eating and drinking of the altar: over an offering that is sacrificed together with its libations.
rashi:a3.1: But didn’t Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana, teach: above [11b], that a voluntary burnt offering does not require song, since its time is not fixed.
gershom:a3.1: [“But didn’t Rav Mari teach: ‘Over your burnt offerings…’? Rather, is it not about libations [brought] by themselves?” (Editor’s note: It seems something is missing here, and it should read: One cannot say that they recited song over the libations of the daily offering, since the daily offering had already ceased.) “Since the daily offering had ceased.”]
rashi:a4.1: And can you understand it: that they were saying it as song on Sunday?
tosafot:a4.1: And can you understand it? The song of the day is “The earth is the Lord’s”: and even if libations brought by themselves do require song, that would be the song of the day on which they are brought, and not the song that was fitting for the day the offering itself was brought.
gershom:a4.1: If so: since they could, if they wished, recite song not over an offering, let them recite it over libations too.
rashi:a5.1: It could result in a mishap: for people would come to say that just as libations brought by themselves are optional, so too libations brought with the offering are optional.
gershom:a5.1: It could result in a mishap: for they would think that the law of libations is that they may be offered only with song, [and if there were no Levites they would not offer them; yet these do not require song.
rashi:a7.1: Of our captivity: the exile of Jehoiachin and the craftsmen and the smiths; and Ezekiel was among them.
gershom:a6.1: “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity”: of the exile of Jeconiah; “fourteen years after the city was smitten”: of the exile of Zedekiah.
rashi:a7.2: Jubilee: its New Year is on Yom Kippur, when the court sounds the shofar, slaves go free to their homes and fields return to their owners, and then it becomes evident that it is a Jubilee. Evidently the Jubilee Year was in the fourteenth year from the destruction of the Temple; and it was assumed that he means counting together with the year of the destruction. And the Jubilee always falls in the year after a Sabbatical Year, since the forty-ninth year is a Sabbatical Year.
gershom:a7.1: For its New Year is on the tenth: for you do not find a New Year day that falls on the tenth except the Jubilee, on Yom Kippur. Evidently, in the fourteenth year it was a Jubilee.
rashi:a8.1: And if it enters your mind that it was destroyed in the year after the Sabbatical Year: how can you find fourteen [years to the Jubilee], counting together [with the year of destruction], if it was in the year after a Sabbatical Year, the first of the cycle, and so on.
tosafot:a8.1: From the first of the cycle to the first of the cycle: he counts fifteen years backward.
gershom:a8.1: And if it enters your mind that it was destroyed in the first of the cycle: from the first of the cycle to the first of the third cycle makes fifteen, and the Jubilee would not arrive until the fifteenth year. Rather, conclude from it: since the verse says “in the fourteenth year” and no more, and that was a Jubilee, you cannot find it unless the Temple was destroyed in the second year of the cycle, and then the Jubilee arrives in the fourteenth year.
rashi:a9.1: After the year: and when you count fifteen years backward from the Jubilee Year, you find the destruction in the year after a Sabbatical Year, which is the thirty-sixth year in the count of this Jubilee.
tosafot:a9.1: Ravina said: “in the fourteenth after the year the city was smitten,” [that is,] in the fifteenth year from the destruction; then was the Jubilee.
gershom:a9.1: Ravina said: Actually it was destroyed in the first of the cycle; and as for your difficulty that the Jubilee would not arrive until the fifteenth, explain it thus: fourteen years after the year it was smitten, which makes fifteen together with that year in which it was smitten.]
rashi:a10.1: If so: that this prophecy was in the fifteenth year from the destruction, it was the twenty-sixth of the exile of Jehoiachin.
tosafot:a10.1: If so: that it was the fifteenth year from the destruction, then the twenty-five are twenty-six. As the Master says: They were exiled in the seventh, meaning, in the seventh from the subjugation of Jehoiakim, whom he subjugated in the fourth year of his [Jehoiakim’s] reign. And he [Jehoiakim] reigned eleven years, and in that year he [Nebuchadnezzar] killed Jehoiakim and crowned his son Jehoiachin for three months; and at the turn of the year, in that same year, he exiled him to Babylonia, together with the craftsmen and the smiths. That was the exile of Ezekiel.
gershom:a10.1: If so: since you count fourteen apart from that year in which it was destroyed,
gershom:a11.1: it comes to twenty-six, yet it is written “in the twenty-fifth year.”
rashi:a10.2: As the Master says: They were exiled: Israel, with Jehoiachin.
rashi:a10.3: In the seventh: in the seventh year from the subjugation of Jehoiakim.
rashi:a10.4: They were exiled in the eighth: that is, that same exile was in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, since he subjugated Jehoiakim in the second year of his reign, as is explained below.
rashi:a11.1: They were exiled in the eighteenth: with Zedekiah, and that was the destruction of Jerusalem; and that was the eighteenth year from the subjugation of Jehoiakim, which is the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.
tosafot:a11.1: They were exiled in the eighteenth from the subjugation: that is, when the city was smitten.
gershom:a12.1: As the Master says: They were exiled in the seventh, they were exiled in the eighth: seven years after Jehoiakim was exiled, Ezekiel was exiled [with] Jeconiah. [They were exiled in the eighteenth after the exile of Jehoiakim: they were exiled with Zedekiah, and the Temple was destroyed.]
rashi:a12.1: From seven until eighteen: from the seventh year, which is the exile of Ezekiel, until eighteen, which is the destruction of the Temple, is eleven, counting the year in which Ezekiel was exiled and not counting the year of the destruction, which we counted with those from the destruction until the Jubilee; and fifteen from the destruction until the Jubilee, with the year of the destruction and the Jubilee year. It turns out there were twenty-six from the year in which they were exiled until the Jubilee; so how did Ezekiel say that the Jubilee was in the twenty-fifth of our captivity? For it was assumed that he means counting together with the year in which they were exiled.
tosafot:a12.1: From the seventh, in which they were exiled, until the eighteenth, in which the city was destroyed, not counting the eighteenth itself, which belongs to the count of fifteen, is eleven: for the seventh year, in which they were exiled, was the last year of Jehoiakim, and then Zedekiah reigned ten years before the year of the destruction; and with fifteen, that makes twenty-six. Granted, had we said that the fourteen years are counted with the year of the destruction itself, it would work out, since fourteen and eleven are twenty-five; but since he says it was the fifteenth year, it is difficult. One could have answered that the year in which they were exiled was the first year of Zedekiah, so there are only ten years from the exile to the year of the destruction; but he holds as established that this is not so, for the exile was in the very year that is counted for Jehoiakim. If so, there are eleven years.
gershom:a13.1: From seven, when Jeconiah was exiled, until eighteen, when the Temple was destroyed, is eleven years; and fifteen, as you established, “after the year the city was smitten,” makes twenty-six; yet the verse says “in the twenty-fifth of our captivity.” Rather, certainly there were fourteen and no more, making twenty-five years. Ravina could say to you: And according to you, who answered thus, “in the fourteenth,” does it work out that there are twenty-five years and no more? Now, they were [also] exiled in the nineteenth, and perforce it makes twenty-six. Rather, what have you to say, so that it makes twenty-five and no more? Separate from the year in which they were exiled, which is not counted, [so that you subtract] that nineteenth year in which they were exiled, leaving only eighteen; and there are only eleven and fourteen, which make twenty-five.
rashi:a13.1: And according to you: who wants to count the year of the destruction among these fourteen, does it work out well?
rashi:a13.2: Now, they were also exiled in the nineteenth: for this answerer had assumed that there were three exiles, since what is taught, “they were exiled in the eighteenth” and “in the nineteenth,” were two exiles, and he held that the destruction was in the eighteenth. And when you count fourteen as well, together with the year of the destruction and the Jubilee year, you find twenty-six from the exile of Jehoiachin, which was in the seventh year, counting together with the year in which they were exiled.
tosafot:a13.1: And according to you, does it work out well? Now, they were exiled in the nineteenth year, and that is when the city was smitten: from seven to nineteen is twelve, and with fourteen that makes twenty-six. He could have objected according to their own approach, since he thought that the eighteenth and the nineteenth were two exiles: if so, how can it be explained? If it was smitten in the eighteenth, it was not smitten in the nineteenth. But one need not be particular, since it is merely the course of the discussion, and by the conclusion it works out.
rashi:a13.3: Rather, what have you to say: about what Ezekiel says, “in the twenty-fifth year of our captivity”?
rashi:a13.4: Separate from the year when they were exiled: Jehoiachin and Ezekiel.
gershom:a14.1: According to me too: he counts fourteen apart from that year in which they were exiled, which he adds, as we said.
rashi:a14.1: In any case, the nineteenth is difficult for Ravina: for certainly the destruction was at the last exile. And since Ravina said fifteen years until the Jubilee, and from the exile of Jehoiachin until the year of the destruction, which is in the nineteenth, there are eleven, not counting the year in which they were exiled and not counting the year of the destruction, then with the fifteen, that makes twenty-six.
gershom:a15.1: In any case, “they were exiled in the nineteenth” is difficult for Ravina: for if he counts from seven to nineteen, that is twelve, and after that fourteen, making twenty-six, since Ravina adds [a year].
rashi:a15.1: Do you hold there were three exiles: it is the Talmud that answers that what we said above, “they were also exiled in the nineteenth,” is not so, for it was one exile: in the eighteenth from the subjugation of Jehoiakim was the destruction of Jerusalem, which is the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar. Therefore, from seven until nineteen, not counting the year in which Jehoiachin and Ezekiel were exiled and not counting the year of the destruction, and fifteen with the year of the destruction and the Jubilee year, makes twenty-five.
gershom:a16.1: Ravina could say to you: Do you hold there were three exiles? As for what he says, “from seven until eighteen” and “from seven until nineteen,” there were only two exiles: what he says, “they were exiled in the seventh, they were exiled in the eighth,” is one year, and likewise “they were exiled in the eighteenth, they were exiled in the nineteenth” is one year. And the reason he says to him “[do you hold] three exiles” and not “four exiles” is that he was not dealing with the eighth, but said “from seven until eighteen” and “from seven until nineteen.” Therefore he says to him: Do you hold there were three exiles?
gershom:a17.1: The exile [of Jehoiachin] was in the seventh from the subjugation of Jehoiakim, which is the eighth [of the reign] of Nebuchadnezzar; and they were exiled in the exile of Zedekiah in the eighteenth from the subjugation of Jehoiakim, which is the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar. So there were only two exiles, and between the exile of (Jehoiakim) [Jehoiachin] and the exile of Zedekiah there were only eleven years.
rashi:a16.1: As the Master says: in Seder Olam.
rashi:b1.1: He subjugated Jehoiakim: this was not an exile, for he exiled no one; rather, he subjugated him to serve under him. And he served him three years, as it is written (II Kings 24:1): “And Jehoiakim became his servant three years”; and he then rebelled against him for three years. As it is written at the beginning of Daniel: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim … Nebuchadnezzar [came] to Jerusalem.” And it is taught in Seder Olam: Is it possible to say so? But Nebuchadnezzar did not become king until the fourth year of Jehoiakim, as it is written (Jeremiah 25:1): “The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim … that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar.” If so, what does “in the third year” teach? The third year of his rebellion, which is the sixth of his subjugation; and his going to Babylonia, and he crowned Jehoiachin in his place. And it is written at the end of Chronicles: “And at the return of the year,” and so on. Evidently, in the seventh year from the first subjugation of Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin was exiled. And it is written at the end of Kings: “And Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to him,” and so on [in the eighth year of his reign]. Evidently, the seventh from the subjugation of Jehoiakim is the eighth of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign. And that is why we say: in the second year he subjugated Jehoiakim.
gershom:b1.1: [And likewise in the Second: at the destruction of the Second Temple, they were exiled in the year after a Sabbatical Year and at the conclusion of Shabbat.
rashi:b3.1: Four hundred and twenty: complete, apart from the year in which it was destroyed.
rashi:b3.2: It was the sixth of the Sabbatical cycle: the 420 years were completed, and it was destroyed in the Sabbatical Year itself.
tosafot:b3.1: It was the sixth of the cycle: meaning, the count of 420 years ended in the sixth of the cycle, and the destruction was in year 421. For so the passage shows, that the Second [Temple] was not destroyed until year 421; whereas the First Temple, which stood 410 years, was destroyed in year 410 itself, as the whole passage shows. It turns out the Temple was destroyed at the beginning of the Jubilee, that is, in the Jubilee Year itself, since the destruction was in year 410. [So] Rashi.
rashi:b4.1: The fiftieth year counts: for the Jubilee Year, and it is the beginning of the next Jubilee. Therefore, according to Rabbi Yehuda, each Jubilee has only forty-nine years.
gershom:b2.1: Counts for here and for there: for the Jubilee, and to be counted as the first year of the next cycle.
rashi:b5.1: If like Rabbi Yehuda: you explain this statement of Rabbi Yosei, then regarding the First, you do not find that the First Temple was destroyed in the year after a Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b3.1: If like Rabbi Yehuda you explain it, then regarding the First you do not find it, according to the reasoning that it was destroyed in the year after a Sabbatical Year.
rashi:b5.2: Seventeen Jubilees: this comes from the verses, as it is written (I Kings 6:1): “And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year…” Subtract the forty of the wilderness, and it turns out that they entered the land 440 years before the building of the Temple; and the First Temple stood 410. That makes 850, which is seventeen Jubilees of fifty.
rashi:b5.3: And you cannot say from the time they entered: the land they counted Sabbatical Years and Jubilees, for if so, the Temple was destroyed at the beginning of the Jubilee, that is, in the Jubilee Year itself. For one cannot say that it was not destroyed until the fifty-first [year], since then our passage would not hold: when you subtract the seven of conquest and the seven of division, you would find the destruction in year thirty-seven of the Jubilee, which is the second of the Sabbatical cycle, whereas we need the year after a Sabbatical Year. Therefore this “beginning of the Jubilee” is explained to us as the Jubilee Year itself. And you do not find that the Jubilee would be “fourteen years after the city was smitten,” as it is written in Ezekiel (40).
rashi:b6.1: Remove from them the seven when they conquered, and so on: and they did not count Sabbatical Years and Jubilees until after fourteen [years]; [and so] you find the Jubilee Year fourteen years after the city was smitten, as Ravina explained above. For when you subtract fourteen from fifty, thirty-six remain; it turns out the Temple was destroyed in the thirty-sixth year, which is the year after a Sabbatical Year, and the Jubilee Year came fourteen years later, apart from the year of the destruction. But if this statement of Rabbi Yosei above follows Rabbi Yehuda, bring seventeen years from the seventeen Jubilees and add them, that is, throw them onto the Jubilees; subtract fourteen of these seventeen for the seven of conquest and the seven of division, and three remain. It turns out it was destroyed in the third of the Sabbatical cycle.
tosafot:b6.1: Rather, remove from them the seven when they conquered and the seven when they divided: and thirty-six remain, and in that year the city was destroyed, which is the year after a Sabbatical Year. But if it follows Rabbi Yehuda, bring seventeen from the seventeen Jubilees, which makes fifty-three years: it would be the third of the Sabbatical cycle. And by the same token he could have objected according to Rabbi Yehuda: if so, how do you find the verse in Ezekiel, that it was [the Jubilee] in the fourteenth from the destruction?
gershom:b4.1: As it is taught: Israel counted seventeen Jubilees from when they entered the land until they left, as it is written: “And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt,” and so on. Remove from them the forty years that they were in the wilderness, and 440 remain; and the Temple stood 410: that makes seventeen Jubilees. It turns out the Temple was destroyed at the beginning of the eighteenth Jubilee, and by this calculation you do not find that in the fourteenth year after the city was smitten it was a Jubilee, as it says, “at the beginning of the year, on the tenth,” and so on. Rather, remove from them the seven when they conquered and the seven when they divided, as is explained below, that they counted Jubilees only from fourteen years after they entered the land; and then you find that fourteen [years] after the city was smitten it was a Jubilee.
gershom:b5.1: And if it follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says the fiftieth year counts for here and for there: bring seventeen from the seventeen Jubilees and set fourteen of them against the fourteen in which they conquered and divided. Three years remain; it turns out it was destroyed in the third of the cycle, and you also do not find that fourteen [years] after its destruction was a Jubilee.]
rashi:b8.1: [Rashi’s text first reads “those three years”; at the end he argues that “three” is a corruption, and the Davidson English follows the reading he adopts.] And he answers: Those three years from when Sennacherib exiled them until Jeremiah came and returned them, and so on: that is, those three years in which Sennacherib besieged them, as it is written (II Kings 17:5): “Then the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land, and went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years.” They had no opportunity to plow and sow and did not count Sabbatical Years and Jubilees, so he does not count them. And what it says, “until Jeremiah came and returned them,” is not precise, for it was more than ninety years from Hezekiah, when Sennacherib exiled them, until Jeremiah returned them in the days of Josiah. Rather, this is what it means: the three years in which Sennacherib exiled them, and they remained in that exile until Jeremiah returned them; those three years are not counted. So I heard. But there are many objections to this. First, when you subtract three years, you find the destruction in year forty-nine, which is a Sabbatical Year, whereas we need the year after a Sabbatical Year; and further, you do not find that fourteen years after the city was smitten was a Jubilee. And one cannot say that Rabbi Yehuda does not accept this exposition, for it is an explicit verse; and below, we find the seven years of division only from this exposition, that fourteen [years] after the city was smitten was a Jubilee. Further, it is difficult for me: why do we subtract only those three years? Don’t we say in the last chapter (below, Arakhin 32b): Once the tribe of Reuben and Gad were exiled, the Jubilees ceased, until Jeremiah returned them? And although we answer there that they counted Jubilees in order to sanctify the Sabbatical Years, that is only according to the Rabbis; but according to Rabbi Yehuda we establish there that they did not count Jubilees at all. Further, how is it possible to take out three years alone? If, when Sennacherib came up against them, they had already counted ten or twelve years of the Jubilee, and he came up against them for three years, how is it possible to skip those three years and return to their original count, and count thirteen, fourteen, to sanctify the Jubilee in the fifty-third year? Perforce they then began to count one, two, three, four. From all these considerations it seems to me that this “three” written in the books is an error, and a mistaken explanation was written into the books. This is how we read: “Those years from when Sennacherib exiled them until Jeremiah came and returned them are not counted,” and it is stated precisely: all those years that they were in exile, Rabbi Yehuda does not count in the count of Sabbatical Years and Jubilees, as we say in the last chapter. Rather, in the year when they returned, in the days of Josiah, they began to count for the Jubilee. Go and count from that year until year 410, the destruction, and you will find your calculation laid out neatly: in the thirty-sixth year of the Jubilee the Temple was destroyed, which is the year after a Sabbatical Year, and you find that fourteen years after the city was smitten was the Jubilee Year. For they returned in the eighteenth year of Josiah, as it is written (II Kings 22) that in the eighteenth year of Josiah the book was found in the Temple, and concerning the words of the book the king sent to Ḥulda the prophetess. And we say in Megilla (14b): How could he pass over Jeremiah and send to Ḥulda? And we say: Jeremiah was not there, for he had gone to bring back the ten tribes. And from where do we know that they returned? As it is written: “What is this monument,” and so on. And this matter, Josiah’s clearing away of idolatry, was in that year. And so I found in Seder Olam: in the eighteenth year of Josiah was the beginning of the Jubilee. Josiah reigned thirty-one years; from eighteen to thirty-one, how many are there? Fourteen; and eleven for Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin, and eleven for Zedekiah, as it is written (II Kings 25:27): that makes thirty-six, and then the Temple was destroyed. So it fits well according to Rabbi Yehuda. This I understood from my own heart, and it was right in my eyes, though I had not heard it [from my teachers]; and afterward I found an old, corrected book in which it is written so, and I told my teachers, and it was right in their eyes.
tosafot:b8.1: Those years in which Sennacherib exiled them: and we do not read “three years,” for there were many: from the sixth of Hezekiah until the seventeenth of Josiah, when Jeremiah returned them, is close to a hundred years. And Rashi further objected to this wording [with three], and it is an error.
tosafot:b8.2: Those years from when Sennacherib exiled them until Jeremiah came and returned them are not counted: and he returned them in the eighteenth of Josiah. Count fourteen of Josiah, who reigned thirty-one, and twenty-two of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah: that makes thirty-six years, and in the thirty-sixth year it was destroyed. And if you ask: if so, what does the baraita mean, “If you say they counted from when they entered, the Temple turns out to have been destroyed at the beginning of the Jubilee”? That is not so, for when they were exiled they stopped counting Jubilees, and when they were returned they resumed counting and sanctifying, and there were only thirty-six years until the destruction. My teacher says that that baraita follows the Rabbis, who say that the fiftieth year is not part of the count of the Sabbatical cycles. According to them, when they were exiled, granted they did not count Jubilees, but they did count and sanctify Sabbatical Years, and they would count Jubilees in order to sanctify the Sabbatical Years by them, as it is at the end of our tractate: they counted Jubilees only to sanctify the Sabbatical Years. If so, when Jeremiah returned them, they did not begin counting from the start of a Jubilee, but continued the same count they had been counting. That is why it says that if they counted from when they entered, the Temple was destroyed in a Jubilee Year. But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says the fiftieth year itself is part of the count of the Sabbatical cycles, in the years that the ten tribes were exiled they counted neither Sabbatical Years nor Jubilees at all; if so, when Jeremiah returned them and the Jubilee was in force, they had to start their count over.
gershom:b6.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “those three years”; the Davidson English, following the Vilna text, omits “three.”] Those three years: he takes them out, corresponding to those three years from when Sennacherib exiled them until Jeremiah came and returned them, (as we translate) [as we read] in the last chapter: this teaches that Jeremiah returned them. He does not count them because Israel was not on its land, and they did not count Jubilees until they returned, as it is written: “And proclaim liberty throughout the land unto all the inhabitants thereof”: when all its inhabitants are upon it. My teacher told us that these three years in which he exiled them we do not find explicitly in Scripture; rather, they relied on the verse that is written: “[And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel,] that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it, and at the end of three years they took it, [in the sixth year of Hezekiah].” It turns out that when he takes out these three years, it was [destroyed] in the year after a Sabbatical Year; [but you do not find a Jubilee fourteen years later, according to Rabbi Yehuda’s reasoning.
rashi:b9.1: And if you wish, say: actually, according to the Rabbis, Rabbi Yosei stated his teaching; and as for your difficulty above, that it was the sixth of the cycle,
rashi:b9.2: when it teaches “and likewise for the Second,” it refers to the rest: to the Ninth of Av and the conclusion of Shabbat.
gershom:b7.1: If you wish, say: actually you can explain it according to the Rabbis, and “and likewise for the Second”: as for your difficulty that six remain, they did not say “and likewise” about the year after a Sabbatical Year, but about the rest: the Ninth of Av and the conclusion of Shabbat.
tosafot:b10.1: Was the watch of Jehoiarib present in the Second? Rabbeinu Elḥanan objected: But we say in Bava Kamma (110a): He gives the money to Jedaiah and the guilt offering to Jehoiarib; evidently it existed in the Second Temple. One can say that that mishna was taught with reference to the time close to the First Temple. Alternatively, not Jehoiarib precisely, but the watch in place of Jehoiarib.
rashi:b11.1: Ascended from the exile: in the days of Ezra.
rashi:b11.2: Jedaiah, Harim, Pashḥur and Immer: for in the First Temple the watch of Jedaiah came before Harim, the watch of Harim before Pashḥur, and that of Pashḥur before Immer.
gershom:b8.1: Four watches ascended from the exile: with Ezra, and no more.]
rashi:b11.3: Divided them into twenty-four watches: and they did not know how to order them, who would serve after whom.
rashi:b11.4: Mixed them up: they wrote the names of the twenty-four watches on twenty-four slips.
rashi:b11.5: And put them in a receptacle: and Jedaiah directed [his hand] by the holy spirit, and his own slip came up in his hand; he put his hand in again and took a slip, and so on six times. And in the order in which the slips came up in his hand, so they set those written on the slips after him, one after another.
